It can provide a set or varying p.d. output, which becomes the input for a further circuit, or it can be used in making measurements of p.d. or resistance. 23.10.1 The Potential Divider Circuit The circuit in Figure contains two resistors, R1 and R2. The voltmeter has an extremely high resistance, so we can ignore the tiny current that flows through it. R1 and R2 are in series. This tells us that we can use the relationship 𝑅 = 𝑅1 + 𝑅2. It also tells us that the same current passes through both R1 and R2. Finally, the p.d.s across R1 and R2 add up to give the total p.d. across the circuit, i.e., 𝑉 = 𝑉1 + 𝑉2 .

23.10.2 Potential Dividers as Sensors The use of the potential divider is in sensor circuits. If the variable resistor, R2, in the potential divider circuit shown in the figure is replaced with a component whose resistance varies with an external physical variable such as temperature or light intensity, then the potential difference across the fixed resistor, R1, will also vary with the external physical variable.
Physics, Grade 11 | 447

The voltmeter connected across R1 can then be calibrated in terms of the value of the external physical variable. The circuit can then be made to act as an electronic thermometer or an electronic light sensor. With an electronic thermometer, a thermistor is connected in place of R2. Most thermistors are NTC (negative temperature coefficient) thermistors. This means that as the temperature increases, their resistance decreases, as shown in figure, which also shows a circuit diagram showing how the components are connected:

The effect on the potential difference across the fixed resistor R1 is that as the temperature increases, so the resistance of the thermistor, R2, drops and V1 rises. Thus, increasing temperature produces increasing p.d. If the voltmeter is connected across the thermistor, the opposite will happen: increasing the temperature will produce a decrease in p.d. In most cases, applications require the p.d. to increase with temperature, so the voltmeter is usually connected across the fixed resistor. A similar effect involves the use of a light-dependent resistor (LDR). These are components that change their resistance with light intensity, which makes them incredibly useful as light sensors. LDRs are made of semi-conducting materials; as the light shines on the material, electrons are freed from the structure and can flow through it, reducing the resistance of the LDR. In the dark, LDRs can have very high resistance, of the order of megaohms, and yet in the light, their resistance can drop as low as a few hundred ohms. If an LDR is connected to a potential divider in place of R2 in the potential divider circuit then, as the light intensity increases, then so will the output p.d. V1 across the fixed resistor.
